newsitem.title: UK: British newspaper rivals battle over audit figures.
newsitem.headline: British newspaper rivals battle over audit figures.

text.p: British newspaper arch-rivals the Times and the Telegraph are continuing to do battle over circulation figures -- with the Times vowing to lodge a formal complaint with the Audit Bureau of Circulation (ABC).

At issue is the audit bureau's decision to allow the inclusion of certain subscription sales of the Daily Telegraph and Sunday Telegraph newspapers -- owned by Canada's Hollinger International Inc -- in its circulation reports.

"Whatever the Telegraph may claim in the recent controversy, the issue of whether or not the Telegraph is breaching the ABC rules in the reporting of its subscription sales figures is far from over," the Times said in a statement.

The Times, owned by media magnate Rupert Murdoch's News Corp Ltd, said it is lodging a formal complaint with the ABC and is also prepared to take legal action. The Times claims the ABC is violating its own by-laws by allowing the inclusion of certain subscription sales of the Telegraph newspapers in circulation figures.
The Telegraph on Tuesday responded by saying that "in our view we've won this."
The Audit Bureau, the likely target of any legal action by the Times, said it was too early to comment.

The Daily Telegraph continues to be Britain's largest circulating broadsheet daily newspaper, and the only weekday broadsheet with circulation topping one million. The Times, meanwhile, has been aggressively fighting to boost its circulation and topple the Telegraph from the No. 1 spot.

Recent circulation promotions by the Times include a 10 pence cover price for the Times on Mondays -- a policy Murdoch has vowed to continue -- as well as a highly successful promotion that ended in late November for free tickets on the cross-Channel Eurostar train.
The Sunday Times is the largest circulating broadsheet newspaper on Sundays.

Sources on either side of the dispute claim on one hand that the Telegraph is fighting to hang onto its much-vaunted one million-plus daily circulation figure, while those on the other side insist that the Times is seeking to cushion an expected sharp drop-off in its December circulation figures following the end of the Eurostar promotion.

The circulation dispute dates to November, when the ABC ruled that discounted subscription sales of the Daily Telegraph and Sunday Telegraph would not be included in the bureau's "full price" category. Although the ABC earlier had agreed to include the figures after the Telegraph objected to its decision, it later backtracked when the Times responded with its own objection.
The ABC omitted circulation figures for the Telegraph when it published its November figures last month, as it reviewed how the figures should be reported.
In late December the ABC said it had decided to include the disputed Telegraph subscription sales for the month of November, calling the issue a "misunderstanding."

"The misunderstanding has now been clarified," the ABC said in a statement. "The Daily Telegraph and Sunday Telegraph have resubmitted their returns to ABC, and the executive committee of the ABC has agreed to those copies sold through subscription being included in the 'full price' category."

The ABC said its decision reflected a finding that there are inconsistencies of how various newspaper represent their subscription copies in the monthly figures. The bureau said publishers who wish for their subscription sales to be included in the "full price" category may resubmit their returns.
The ABC will publish the November circulation figures for the Daily Telegraph and Sunday Telegraph later this week when it also issues circulation figures for the month of December.

The Telegraph spokesman said the newspaper estimates the Daily Telegraph in November had circulation of 1,101,000, including 100,000 subscription sales at the heart of the dispute. It estimates its December circulation at 1,132,000.
The Times in November had audited circulation of 861,931.
